questions.q: What makes a webhook different from a normal API call?
options: Webhooks don't use JSON
The provider's server calls your server, instead of you calling theirs
Webhooks never include a request body
Webhooks only work over FTP
questions.explain: A webhook reverses the normal direction: the provider POSTs an event to a URL you registered, rather than you initiating the request.

questions.q: In a webhook event payload like Stripe's, what does the "type" field tell your handler?
options: The HTTP status code to respond with
The size of the payload in bytes
Which kind of event occurred, so your handler knows how to react
The signing secret to use
questions.explain: type identifies the event (e.g. "payment_intent.succeeded"), which a handler typically switches on to decide what to do.

questions.q: Why must a webhook handler verify the signature header before trusting the payload?
options: Signature verification is optional and mostly for logging
Anyone who discovers the webhook URL could POST fake JSON to it; the signature proves it genuinely came from the provider
It speeds up JSON parsing
It's required only in test mode
questions.explain: A public webhook URL can be POSTed to by anyone — signature verification is what proves a given payload is authentic and untampered.

questions.q: Why should a webhook handler return a 2xx response quickly, before doing slow work?
options: 2xx responses are cached by the provider
Slow responses get logged as warnings but otherwise don't matter
It reduces the payload size
If the response takes too long, the provider may treat delivery as failed and retry, risking duplicate processing
questions.explain: Providers expect a fast acknowledgment; a slow or missing 2xx can trigger retries of the same event.

questions.q: What does Stripe's Stripe-Signature header's "t" value represent?
options: The event type
The total number of retries so far
A timestamp, included in the signed payload to prevent replay attacks
A test/live mode flag
questions.explain: t is the timestamp used (along with the raw body) to compute the HMAC signature, and it's also checked against a tolerance window to guard against replay attacks.
